titulo: So that they ask you back
subtitulo: The ten minutes between the first goodbye and the door, the eight words that get a bar to remember you next year, and the pocket list of everything this course would keep if it could only keep twelve things
cena: Half eleven on your last night, the table has been saying goodbye for ten minutes and nobody has stood up, and the man who poured your coffee every morning is behind the bar.
decisao: whether the last five minutes of the trip buy you a face they know next year, or you leave the way most visitors leave — through the door, with a nod
permissao: You are allowed to say you will be back without naming a month. Nobody is holding you to a date, and the sentence is heard as warmth, not as a booking. You are allowed to leave a place you loved without a speech: eight words at the counter do more than a card and a big tip. And you are allowed to finish this course still getting the endings the other way round — guiri is said with affection far more often than not, and the one they remember is the one who said goodbye properly, not the one who said it perfectly.
espelho: The 'we must do this again sometime' you say at your own front door and never mean is the bit that reads as odd there. Said in Spain it is taken at face value, and somebody will ask you which weekend.
frasePiso: You will say goodbye to a Spanish bar in a way that gets you a face they know next year. Most visitors spend a fortnight in the same place and leave through the door with a nod.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Somebody says they are going, and eleven minutes later everybody is still sitting down, saying they are going again.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They are being polite about wanting to leave, and one of us should be brave and stand up first.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The goodbye is a stretch of the evening rather than a moment in it. It opens with a 'bueno', it runs on the same warmth as the rest of the night, and standing up on the first one ends the evening ten minutes early for everybody.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Announce it, then stay in your chair and keep talking until the others start moving. Leave when the third goodbye happens, not the first.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the best ten minutes of the night — the ones where people say the things they did not say over dinner — instead of standing in a doorway with your coat on.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not where a clock is running the room. A work lunch ends, a bar putting the chairs up ends, and a last metro ends — there the first goodbye is the real one and nobody is offended by it.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You are leaving and somebody hands you an open invitation with no date on it — come back, you know where we are.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: That is the polite noise people make at a door. It means nothing and I am not meant to act on it.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Said to somebody who has been in and out all week, it is closer to an address being handed over than to a pleasantry. Nobody expects a date; they do expect the sentence to be true.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Answer it as though it were a plan rather than a compliment — say when you are next in the country, even if the when is a year away.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You come back and you are a face they know, which is the difference between being served and being greeted.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not 'hasta luego' from a shop assistant or a chemist. That one is simply the word for bye, it is said to people who will never be seen again, and it promises nothing at all.

fichasCulturais.sinal: On the last morning you pay for the coffee, nod at the man who has made it every day since Monday, and he nods back and turns to the machine.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: We had a week of something and he did not care either way. I was the tourist and now I am gone.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: He does not know it is the last one. The week of small greetings only becomes a week to him at the point somebody says out loud that it is ending, and almost no visitor ever says it.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Say it is the last morning, say how the week was, and say you will be back — three short sentences, standing at the counter, with the case by the door.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The goodbye you get back is a different size from the nod, and next year the second coffee tends to arrive without being asked for.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in a place with a rota of twenty and a queue behind you. There nobody has served you all week — nobody has served you twice — and a nod is the whole of what is on offer.

aprofundar.titulo: The long goodbye, the open invitation, and the twelve things (optional reading)

secoes.titulo: Why the goodbye takes ten minutes
secoes.corpo: The thing to notice is not that people are slow to leave — it is that leaving is treated as a stretch of the evening with its own shape, rather than as the moment the evening stops. It opens with somebody saying 'bueno', usually with a hand on a knee, and 'bueno' here is doing the work that a chair scraping does elsewhere: it announces, and nothing more. What follows is a run of second thoughts, last stories and the things nobody said over dinner, and it is very often the best part of the night. Then somebody actually stands, and the whole table moves at once. If you get up on the first 'bueno' you have not been efficient, you have taken the last ten minutes off five people, and the evening ends looking like a meeting. The practical version: announce it, stay seated, and leave when the second or third goodbye comes round. Useful noises for the run-up, none of which you have to produce: 'venga' (come on, right then), 'que ya es tarde' (it's late now), 'que mañana madrugo' (I've an early start). The exceptions are all clock-shaped — a work lunch, a bar stacking chairs, a last metro — and there the first goodbye is the real one.

exemplos.pt: BWEH-noh, pwehs NAH-dhah — 👂 right then, well — the opening of the goodbye, not the end of it
BEN-gah — 👂 come on, I've an early start tomorrow

secoes.titulo: 'Hasta luego', 'hasta la próxima' and 'nos vemos' are three different sizes
secoes.corpo: 'Hasta luego' looks as though it means 'see you later' and commits you to a time. It does not. It is the ordinary word for bye, it is said walking out of a shop to somebody you will never see again, and it is what you say nine times a day for a fortnight. 'Adiós' does the same job and is slightly flatter; in some places it is even used as a greeting in passing. 'Hasta la próxima' — until the next time — is a size up: it is for somebody you have had a week with, and it says there will be a next time. 'Nos vemos' is the same weight and looser in shape: 'nos vemos el año que viene', 'nos vemos en septiembre', 'nos vemos pronto'. And 'que os vaya bien' — or 'que te vaya bien' to one person — is a wish rather than a farewell, said to people who are going off to do something: a shift, a drive, the rest of their week. All of these are learnt whole. Nothing inside them needs to be worked out at a door and nothing inside them ever gets taken apart: 'que te vaya bien' and 'que os vaya bien' are two separate things to carry, one aimed at a person and one at a pair.

exemplos.pt: nohs BEH-mohs en sep-TYEM-breh — see you in September
keh teh BAH-yah byen — all the best (to one person)

secoes.titulo: The open invitation, and taking it at face value
secoes.corpo: 'Cuando volváis, ya sabéis dónde estamos' — whenever you're back, you know where we are — is not a form of words to be nodded at. In a bar or a shop you have used every day for a week, it is closer to an address being handed over: no date is expected, but the sentence is meant, and answering it with a thank you rather than a when is a small missed opportunity. The reply that works is a plan without a diary entry: 'nos vemos el año que viene'. It costs nothing, it is heard as true, and it is the reason the second coffee turns up unasked the following summer. This runs exactly opposite to the British habit of saying 'we must do this again sometime' as a way of ending a conversation. Said in Spain, that sentence is taken literally, and the honest thing is either to mean it or to use a smaller goodbye instead. One more that belongs in the same drawer: if somebody says 'a ver si nos vemos' — let's see if we can meet up — that is a genuine, if soft, opening, and the way to accept it is to name something, however small.

exemplos.pt: ah behr see nohs BEH-mohs — 👂 let's see if we can meet up — soft, and real
yah sah-BAIS DHON-deh ehs-TAH-mohs — 👂 you know where we are

secoes.titulo: Saying goodbye to the people who served you all week
secoes.corpo: The counter you stood at every morning is the cheapest relationship of the trip and the one most visitors leave without touching. The reason is structural rather than rude: he does not know it is your last day. A week of nods only becomes a week at the moment somebody says out loud that it is ending. Three short sentences do all of it, standing up, with the case by the door: 'Mañana nos vamos' — we leave tomorrow; 'Ha estado genial' — it's been great; 'Volveré' or 'nos vemos el año que viene'. Add 'gracias por la paciencia con mi español' for whoever slowed down for you and never switched to English, and expect to be told your Spanish is excellent, which it is not and which is not the point. If you were served by two people, 'que os vaya muy bien' takes them both at once. None of this is a speech: the whole thing is under fifteen seconds, and it is the difference between being a customer and being a face. Where it does not apply is a big place with a rota — twenty staff, a queue behind you, nobody who has served you twice. There a nod is genuinely the whole of what is on offer, and nothing has gone wrong.

exemplos.es: Mañana nos vamos. Ha estado genial.
exemplos.pt: mah-NYAH-nah nohs BAH-mohs — we're off tomorrow. It's been great

exemplos.es: Gracias por la paciencia con mi español.
exemplos.pt: pah-THYEN-thyah — thanks for putting up with my Spanish

secoes.corpo: The pocket list, in full, for the screenshot, in the order the recap says it. One: dinner runs from about nine, and last orders are around half eleven; at seven you are having tapas, which is a good evening and not the one you booked. Two: the 'menú del día' at weekday lunch averages about €14.20 and is the best value in the country — and while you are at that table, a free tapa with the drink is a Granada habit rather than a Spanish law, so expect nothing and be pleased by everything. Three: 'una jarra de agua del grifo, por favor' — tap water inside a hospitality business has been free by law since 2022. Four: 'de guardia' is the word — there is no chemist open around the clock on every corner, there is a rota, and tonight's list is posted on the door of the closed one. Five: check the printed price list before you sit on the terrace; bar, table and terrace are legally allowed to cost three different amounts. Six: round up; a fifth does not read as generous. Seven: bag in front of you on the metro and phone off the table, particularly on the busiest lines at rush hour. Eight: do not take the sprig of rosemary — hands in pockets, 'no, gracias', keep walking. Nine: real officers do not ask to see your wallet; 'vamos a la comisaría' ends that conversation. Ten: 'la hoja de reclamaciones, por favor', said calmly and sitting down, settles most arguments before it is ever filled in. Eleven: T-shirt on when you leave the sand, can off the street, and in Barcelona that fine is now taken on the spot, by card. Twelve, and the cheapest of the lot: 'hola' walking in and 'hasta luego' walking out, every door, every time, including the doors you will never walk through again. Rules change, so check the official page before you fly — the links are in the app.

exemplos.es: Una jarra de agua del grifo, por favor.
exemplos.pt: OO-nah KHAH-rrah deh AH-gwah del GREE-foh — a jug of tap water, please

exemplos.es: La hoja de reclamaciones, por favor.
